title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT)
hook: Chop an image into patches, treat each like a word, and feed them to a plain Transformer. With enough pretraining data, it matches or beats convolutional networks.
key_points: Splits an image into fixed-size patches and treats each patch as a token.
Feeds the patch tokens into a standard Transformer encoder, with almost no vision-specific design.
Matches or surpasses strong CNNs when pretrained on large enough datasets.
Needs lots of pretraining data; on small datasets CNNs' built-in biases still win.
content_html: Alexey Dosovitskiy, Lucas Beyer, and colleagues at Google asked whether vision really needs convolutions. The Vision Transformer (ViT) says largely not: cut an image into fixed patches, embed each as a token, and run them through a standard Transformer. Given enough pretraining data, this nearly architecture-agnostic recipe matches or beats top convolutional networks, carrying the Transformer from language into vision.
extra_html:
How it works

ViT divides an image into a grid of small patches — say 16x16 pixels — and flattens each into a vector through a linear projection, producing a sequence of patch tokens. It adds positional embeddings so the model knows where each patch sat, prepends a special classification token, and feeds the whole sequence to a regular Transformer encoder. Self-attention lets every patch attend to every other from the first layer, so the model learns global relationships directly rather than building them up through local convolutions.

Why it matters

Convolutional networks come with strong built-in assumptions about images, like locality, which help when data is limited. ViT drops most of those assumptions and instead learns them from data — which means it needs large-scale pretraining to shine, but then scales gracefully. It unified the architectures behind language and vision, and became the backbone for multimodal models and many later vision systems.

related.title: Attention Is All You Need
related.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

related.title: CLIP: Learning Visual Models from Language
related.hook: Skip the fixed label list. Train on image–caption pairs so pictures and text share one space, and you can classify images from plain-text labels you make up on the spot.

related.title: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet)
related.hook: Stacking more layers used to make networks worse, not better. ResNet's fix — let each layer learn a tweak to its input — unlocked nets over 100 layers deep.

flashcards.prompt: How does ViT turn an image into something a Transformer can process?
flashcards.back_html: It cuts the image into fixed-size patches, linearly projects each into a token vector, adds positional embeddings, and feeds the sequence to a standard Transformer encoder.

flashcards.prompt: Why does ViT need large-scale pretraining to beat CNNs?
